blocks.text: Alternative investments are often defined by exclusion: anything other than long-only positions in **traditional** assets (public equities, investment-grade bonds, cash). It is more useful to describe them by their **characteristics**.

items: **Illiquidity** and long holding periods (private equity, real estate, private debt).
**Less transparency** and less regulation; valuations often appraisal- or model-based.
**Non-normal returns**: skewness, fat tails, autocorrelation (smoothing).
**Active, skill-based management**, use of leverage, short selling and derivatives.
**Specialized structures** (limited partnerships, separately managed accounts) and complex fees.
Market inefficiencies → potential for **alpha**, but also high dispersion of manager returns.

blocks.text: Main categories

head: Category
Examples
rows: Real estate, commodities, infrastructure, farmland, timberland, intellectual property
Macro, managed futures, event-driven, relative value, equity long/short, multistrategy
Venture capital, growth equity, buyouts, secondaries
Direct lending, mezzanine, distressed debt, CLOs

blocks.text: Returns: alpha vs. beta

**Beta** is the return from bearing systematic (market) risk, cheaply available through index products. **Alpha** is return in excess of what is required for the systematic risks borne — it comes from skill, informational advantages or market inefficiencies. Much of what is sold as alpha is actually **alternative beta** (exposure to risk premia such as illiquidity, credit, volatility or carry).
Market efficiency

items: **Informational efficiency**: prices reflect available information (weak, semi-strong, strong forms).

Alternative markets tend to be **less efficient** (private information, illiquidity, high transaction costs), which allows active managers to earn returns — but also makes performance harder to measure.

blocks.text: On the exam, “alternative” is rarely about the asset alone: it is about **how** it is held (illiquid, levered, private, actively managed) and **how returns behave** (non-normal, smoothed).

Retiens la distinction **alpha** (compétence, rendement anormal) / **bêta** (rémunération d’un risque systématique). Les bêtas « alternatifs » (prime d’illiquidité, de crédit, de volatilité) sont souvent vendus comme de l’alpha.

blocks.label: Continuously compounded (log) return
blocks.note: Log returns are **additive over time**: the multi-period log return is the sum of the period log returns.

blocks.text: Arithmetic vs. geometric mean
The **geometric mean** measures compound growth and is always ≤ the arithmetic mean (equal only if returns are constant). The gap grows with volatility: geometric ≈ arithmetic − variance/2.

blocks.title: Volatility drag
lines: USD 100 becomes USD 75: the geometric mean tells the truth.

blocks.text: Time-weighted vs. dollar-weighted returns

head: Time-weighted (TWR)
Dollar-weighted (IRR)
rows: Discount rate that sets NPV of all cash flows to zero
Affected by size and timing of flows
Managers who do **not** control flows (mutual funds, hedge funds)
Managers who **do** control flows (private equity GPs)

blocks.text: Limits of IRR

items: **Multiple or no IRR** when cash flows change sign more than once.
Implicit assumption that interim cash flows are **reinvested at the IRR**.
Ignores **scale**: a high IRR on a small, short deal may create little wealth; early distributions inflate IRR.
Can be managed by the GP (e.g., subscription lines delay capital calls and boost IRR).

blocks.text: A fund with a higher IRR does not necessarily have a higher multiple: quick exits boost IRR while long holds boost the multiple. Always look at both.

**TWR** = performance du gérant indépendamment des flux. **IRR (TRI)** = rendement « vécu » par l’investisseur, sensible au calendrier des flux : c’est la mesure standard en private equity, où le GP décide des appels et des distributions.
Alternative investment returns often violate the assumption of normally distributed, independent returns. Four moments describe a distribution: **mean**, **variance**, **skewness** and **kurtosis**.

head: Feature
Meaning
Typical in
rows: Long left tail: frequent small gains, rare large losses
Merger arbitrage, convertible arbitrage, selling options, credit
Long right tail: frequent small losses, rare large gains
Trend following (managed futures), venture capital, long options
Fat tails and a peaked center: extreme events more likely than under normality
Most hedge fund strategies, commodities, crypto

blocks.text: The normal distribution has skewness 0 and kurtosis 3 (**excess** kurtosis 0). Investors generally like positive skew and dislike fat tails.
Autocorrelation and smoothing

**Autocorrelation** is the correlation of a return series with its own lagged values. Positive autocorrelation in alternative returns usually comes from **smoothing**: stale prices, appraisal-based valuations (real estate, private equity) or managers marking illiquid positions conservatively.

items: Smoothing **understates volatility**, **understates correlation** with markets and beta, and therefore **overstates Sharpe ratios**.
With positive autocorrelation, the square-root-of-time rule **understates** long-horizon volatility.
**Unsmoothing** recovers an estimate of the true return series (see formula).

blocks.text: Correlation, covariance and beta

Correlations of alternatives with equities tend to **rise in crises** (correlation breakdown / contagion), so diversification benefits measured in calm periods may disappear when they are most needed.

Le **lissage** (rendements d’évaluation) donne une volatilité trop faible, une corrélation trop faible et un Sharpe trop élevé. Si une question évoque des prix « d’expert » ou « stale », pense autocorrélation positive.
Because alternative returns are skewed and fat-tailed, standard deviation alone is not enough. The curriculum covers measures of **dispersion**, **downside risk** and **tail risk**.

head: Measure
Definition
rows: Square root of variance; treats upside and downside equally.
Average squared deviation **below the mean** only.
Average squared shortfall below a chosen target (e.g., 0% or the risk-free rate); its square root is the downside deviation used in the Sortino ratio.
Probability that the return falls below a target.
Standard deviation of the return difference between a portfolio and its benchmark.
Loss from a previous peak; maximum drawdown = largest peak-to-trough decline over the period.
Loss that will not be exceeded with a given confidence over a given horizon.
Expected loss **given that** the loss exceeds the VaR.

blocks.label: Parametric (normal) VaR
blocks.note: $z = 1.645$ at 95%, $z = 2.33$ at 99% (one-tailed). For short horizons $\mu$ is often set to zero.

blocks.text: Three ways to compute VaR

items: **Parametric** (variance–covariance): assumes a distribution, usually normal → underestimates tail risk with fat tails.
**Historical simulation**: uses the actual distribution of past returns → no distributional assumption, but depends on the sample.
**Monte Carlo simulation**: simulates many scenarios from a model → flexible (non-linear positions), but model-dependent.

blocks.text: VaR says nothing about **how bad** losses are beyond the threshold, and it is not always subadditive (the VaR of a portfolio can exceed the sum of VaRs). Conditional VaR addresses the first issue.

blocks.title: Square-root-of-time
lines: 10-day VaR ≈ USD 1m × $\sqrt{10}$ = USD 3.16m (valid only if returns are i.i.d.).

blocks.text: VaR à 95 % sur 1 jour de 2 M : on s’attend à perdre **plus** de 2 M un jour sur vingt en moyenne. La CVaR répond à : « et quand ça arrive, combien perd-on en moyenne ? »

fiches.title: Risk-Adjusted Performance Measures
fiches.fr: Mesures de performance ajustées du risque

items: **Sharpe** is appropriate when the portfolio is the investor’s **entire** wealth (total risk matters).
**Treynor** and **Jensen’s alpha** suit a portfolio that is **one part of a diversified** portfolio (only systematic risk matters).
**Sortino** suits skewed returns and investors who care about downside only.
**Information ratio** measures active management skill relative to a benchmark.

blocks.text: Sharpe ratios of smoothed or negatively skewed strategies (e.g., option selling, illiquid assets) are **overstated**: low measured volatility hides tail risk. Sharpe ratios can also be manipulated by changing the measurement frequency.

Leverage financed at the risk-free rate leaves the **Sharpe** and **Treynor** ratios unchanged, because excess return, volatility and beta all scale by the same factor. It does change **Jensen’s alpha** in absolute terms.
Sharpe → risque total ; Treynor → bêta ; Sortino → risque à la baisse ; IR → tracking error. Choisis selon le contexte : portefeuille entier ou poche d’un portefeuille diversifié.

blocks.label: Multi-factor model
blocks.note: Typical factors: market, size (SMB), value (HML), momentum, credit, term, volatility, liquidity.

blocks.text: Ex ante vs. ex post alpha

items: **Ex ante alpha**: expected return above the return required for the risks taken — a forward-looking concept that reflects true skill or mispricing.
**Ex post alpha**: realized return above the benchmark/model return — includes skill **and luck** (and model misspecification).

blocks.text: A positive ex post alpha may just reflect an omitted factor (e.g., a fund long small-cap value stocks measured against a market-only model). Model misspecification creates **false alpha**.
Hypothesis testing

items: State the null hypothesis, e.g., $H_0: \alpha = 0$ (no skill), and the alternative.
Choose a significance level (e.g., 5%).
Compute the test statistic: $t = \hat{\alpha}/SE(\hat{\alpha})$.
Reject $H_0$ if $|t|$ exceeds the critical value (≈ 1.96 for a two-tailed 5% test with many observations), or if the p-value < significance level.

blocks.text: Pitfalls

items: **Data mining / backtest overfitting**: testing many strategies guarantees some look significant by chance.
**Spurious correlation** and non-stationarity: relationships that change over time.
**Survivorship and selection biases** in databases (see hedge funds).
**Non-linear exposures**: option-like payoffs make linear betas misleading; betas can change with market conditions (**beta creep**, asymmetric up/down betas).
**Statistical vs. economic significance**: a significant alpha may be too small to matter after fees.

blocks.text: Erreur de **type I** = conclure à tort qu’un gérant a de l’alpha (faux positif). Erreur de **type II** = passer à côté d’un vrai talent. R² élevé = le modèle explique bien les rendements, ce qui laisse peu de place à l’alpha.

fiches.title: Structures, Fees and Liquidity Terms
fiches.fr: Structures, frais et conditions de liquidité

blocks.text: Most private funds are organized as **limited partnerships**: the **general partner** (GP) manages the fund and has unlimited liability; **limited partners** (LPs) provide capital with liability limited to their investment. Alternatives include separately managed accounts (SMAs), funds of one, UCITS/’40 Act liquid alternatives and evergreen vehicles.
Fee vocabulary

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Annual % of AUM (hedge funds) or of committed/invested capital (PE), e.g., 1.5–2%.
% of profits paid to the manager, e.g., 20%.
Minimum return before incentive fees apply. **Soft hurdle**: once exceeded, the fee applies to all profits (via catch-up). **Hard hurdle**: the fee applies only to returns above the hurdle.
Incentive fees are paid only on gains that take NAV above its previous highest level (losses must be recovered first).
After LPs receive the hurdle, the GP receives a high share of profits until it reaches its full carry percentage.
Obligation for the GP to return carry received in excess of what it is entitled to over the life of the fund.

blocks.label: Incentive fee as a call option
blocks.note: The manager holds a call option on the fund’s value with strike = high-water mark. Its value rises with **volatility**, which can encourage risk-taking, especially when NAV is far below the HWM (option deep out of the money).

blocks.text: Liquidity terms

items: **Lockup**: initial period during which investors cannot redeem (hard lockup) or can redeem only with a penalty (soft lockup).
**Notice period** and **redemption frequency** (monthly, quarterly).
**Gate**: limit on the share of fund assets that can be redeemed in one period.
**Side pocket**: segregated account for illiquid assets; investors only receive value when assets are realized.
**Suspension** of redemptions in extreme cases.

blocks.text: With a high-water mark, a fund that lost 20% last year must gain 25% just to get back to the HWM before charging incentive fees. Managers far below the HWM may close the fund and restart rather than work for free.

La commission de performance est une **option d’achat** détenue par le gérant : asymétrique (il partage les gains mais pas les pertes), elle peut l’inciter à augmenter le risque. Le high-water mark et le co-investissement du gérant limitent ce problème.

formulas.name: Holding period return
formulas.vars: $P_0$ prix initial, $P_1$ prix final, $D$ revenus perçus.

formulas.name: Square-root-of-time rule
formulas.note: Valable si les rendements sont indépendants (i.i.d.).

formulas.name: t-statistic
formulas.note: Rejeter $H_0$ si $|t| > 1{,}96$ (test bilatéral à 5 %, grand échantillon).

cards.back: Return in excess of the return required for the systematic risks borne; attributed to skill, information or mispricing.
Systematic exposure to risk premia other than the equity market (illiquidity, credit, volatility, carry, momentum) that can be mistaken for alpha.

cards.front: Ex ante alpha vs. ex post alpha
cards.back: Ex ante: expected excess return from skill or mispricing. Ex post: realized excess return, which includes luck and model error.
Geometric linking of sub-period returns; not affected by the size or timing of external cash flows.
Dollar-weighted return: the discount rate that makes the NPV of all cash flows equal to zero; sensitive to cash-flow timing.
The gap between arithmetic and geometric mean returns, approximately half the variance; it grows with volatility.
A distribution with a long left tail: frequent small gains and occasional large losses.
Positive excess kurtosis: fatter tails and a more peaked center than the normal distribution.
Correlation between a return series and its own past values; positive autocorrelation often signals smoothing.
Reported returns that adjust slowly to true value changes (stale or appraisal prices), understating volatility and correlation.
The average squared deviation of returns below the mean; target semivariance uses a chosen target instead of the mean.
The probability that a return falls below a specified target level.
The standard deviation of the difference between portfolio and benchmark returns.
The largest peak-to-trough percentage decline in value over a period.
The loss that will not be exceeded with a given confidence level over a given horizon.
The expected loss given that the loss exceeds the VaR threshold.
cards.fr: Perte moyenne au-delà de la VaR.

cards.back: Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by total volatility.
Excess return over the risk-free rate divided by beta; appropriate for a diversified portfolio component.
Return in excess of a target divided by the downside deviation (square root of target semivariance).
Active return (portfolio minus benchmark) divided by tracking error.
Rejecting a true null hypothesis — e.g., concluding a manager has skill when they do not (false positive).
Failing to reject a false null hypothesis — e.g., missing a manager who truly has skill (false negative).
Finding apparently significant results by testing many models or parameters on the same data; results fail out of sample.
The GP manages the partnership and has unlimited liability; LPs provide capital and have liability limited to their investment.
The highest previous NAV; incentive fees are only charged on gains above it.
cards.fr: Plus haut historique de la VL.

cards.back: Soft: once the hurdle is exceeded, the incentive fee applies to all profits. Hard: the fee applies only to profits above the hurdle.
After investors receive the hurdle return, the manager receives most or all of the next profits until reaching its full share of carry.
A provision requiring the GP to return previously received carried interest if, at the end of the fund, it has received more than its agreed share.
A limit on the percentage of a fund’s assets that may be redeemed in a single redemption period.
A separate account within a fund holding illiquid assets; investors receive value only when those assets are realized.
An initial period during which investors cannot redeem (hard) or can redeem only with a penalty (soft).

questions.q: Which characteristic is LEAST typical of alternative investments?
options: Daily liquidity at transparent market prices
questions.explain: La liquidité quotidienne à des prix de marché transparents caractérise les actifs **traditionnels**. Les alternatifs sont typiquement illiquides, avec des rendements non normaux et des frais complexes.

questions.q: A private credit fund earns 3% per year above public high-yield bonds, mainly by holding illiquid loans. This excess return is best described as:
options: Pure ex ante alpha from skill
questions.explain: Être rémunéré pour porter de l’**illiquidité** est un bêta alternatif (prime de risque systématique), pas forcément de l’alpha issu du talent.

questions.q: The main difference between ex ante alpha and ex post alpha is that ex post alpha:
options: Includes the effects of luck and model misspecification
Is always larger than ex ante alpha
questions.explain: L’alpha **ex post** est réalisé : il mélange talent, chance et erreurs de modèle. L’alpha **ex ante** est l’espérance de rendement anormal.

questions.q: An asset rises 50% in year 1 and falls 50% in year 2. What is the geometric average annual return?
questions.explain: $(1{,}5 \times 0{,}5)^{1/2} - 1 = \sqrt{0{,}75} - 1 = -13{,}4\%$. La moyenne arithmétique (0 %) surestime : 100 devient 75.

questions.q: Which statement about continuously compounded returns is correct?
options: They can be summed across periods to obtain the multi-period continuously compounded return
They are always larger than simple returns
They must be multiplied across periods
questions.explain: Les rendements log sont **additifs dans le temps**. Ils sont inférieurs aux rendements simples quand R > 0, et peuvent être négatifs.

questions.q: Which return measure is most appropriate to evaluate a private equity GP who controls the timing of capital calls and distributions?
questions.explain: Quand le gérant **contrôle les flux**, le rendement pondéré par les capitaux (**IRR**) mesure correctement sa décision. Le TWR convient aux gérants qui subissent les flux (fonds ouverts, hedge funds).

questions.q: Which is a known limitation of the IRR?
options: Cash flows that change sign more than once can produce multiple IRRs
It ignores the timing of cash flows
It cannot be computed for private equity funds
It always equals the time-weighted return
questions.explain: Avec plusieurs changements de signe des flux, l’IRR peut avoir **plusieurs solutions** (ou aucune). Il suppose aussi un réinvestissement au taux de l’IRR et ignore l’échelle.

questions.q: A GP starts using a subscription credit line to fund investments and calls LP capital six months later. All else equal, the most likely effect is:
options: A higher IRR with little change in the multiple
A lower IRR and a higher multiple
No effect on IRR because cash flows are unchanged
A lower multiple and a lower IRR
questions.explain: Retarder les appels de fonds raccourcit la durée pendant laquelle le capital des LP est investi : l’**IRR augmente**, alors que le multiple change peu (il baisse même un peu à cause des intérêts de la ligne).

questions.q: A return distribution with frequent small gains and occasional large losses is said to have:
questions.explain: Petits gains fréquents + grosses pertes rares = longue queue à gauche = **asymétrie négative** (ex. arbitrage de fusion, vente d’options).

questions.q: A normal distribution has an excess kurtosis of:
questions.explain: La kurtosis d’une loi normale vaut 3, donc la kurtosis **excédentaire** (kurtosis − 3) vaut 0.

questions.q: Which strategy is most likely to exhibit positive skewness?
questions.explain: Le **suivi de tendance** ressemble à une position longue en options (straddle) : petites pertes fréquentes, gros gains rares → asymétrie **positive**. Les trois autres ont une asymétrie négative.

questions.q: Returns of an appraisal-based real estate index display strong positive first-order autocorrelation. Compared with true underlying returns, the reported series most likely:
options: Understates volatility and correlation with equities
questions.explain: Le **lissage** (évaluations d’experts) sous-estime la volatilité et la corrélation, et **surestime** donc le ratio de Sharpe.

questions.q: A private equity index reports +4% this quarter and +2% last quarter. The estimated first-order autocorrelation is 0.5. What is the unsmoothed return for this quarter?
If monthly returns are positively autocorrelated, scaling monthly volatility by $\sqrt{12}$ will:
options: Have no effect because autocorrelation only affects the mean
questions.explain: La règle de la racine du temps suppose l’indépendance. Avec une **autocorrélation positive**, les mouvements se cumulent : la volatilité annuelle réelle est **plus élevée** que σ√12.

questions.q: A fund has a volatility of 12%, the market a volatility of 16%, and their correlation is 0.6. What is the fund’s beta?
questions.explain: $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_i/\sigma_m = 0{,}6 \times 12/16 = 0{,}45$.

questions.q: Why may diversification benefits from hedge funds and other alternatives be weaker than historical correlations suggest?
options: Correlations tend to increase during market crises
Correlations are always negative in crises
Correlation does not affect portfolio risk
questions.explain: Les corrélations **augmentent en période de crise** (contagion, liquidations forcées), justement quand la diversification serait la plus utile.

questions.q: Which risk measure considers only returns below a target level?
questions.explain: La **semi-variance cible** ne retient que les écarts au-dessous de la cible. L’écart-type traite hausses et baisses de la même façon.

questions.q: A fund’s NAV goes from 100 to 140, then down to 98, then up to 120. Its maximum drawdown is:
A USD 50 million portfolio has a daily volatility of 1%. Assuming normality and a zero mean, what is the one-day 99% VaR (z = 2.33)?
The one-day 95% VaR of a position is USD 2 million. Assuming i.i.d. returns, its 25-day 95% VaR is closest to:
questions.explain: $2 \times \sqrt{25} = 2 \times 5 = 10$ M USD (règle de la racine du temps).

questions.q: Which statement about parametric (normal) VaR is most accurate for a portfolio of hedge funds with fat-tailed returns?
options: It is likely to underestimate tail losses
It is likely to overestimate tail losses
It is unaffected by the shape of the distribution
questions.explain: Avec des **queues épaisses**, les pertes extrêmes sont plus fréquentes que ce que prévoit la loi normale : la VaR paramétrique **sous-estime** le risque de queue.

questions.q: Conditional VaR (expected shortfall) differs from VaR because it:
options: Measures the average loss in the cases where losses exceed the VaR
Measures the probability of exceeding the VaR
questions.explain: La **CVaR** est la perte moyenne au-delà du seuil de VaR. Elle est toujours supérieure ou égale à la VaR au même niveau de confiance.

questions.q: Which VaR method makes no assumption about the shape of the return distribution but depends heavily on the sample period used?
questions.explain: La **simulation historique** utilise directement les rendements passés : pas d’hypothèse de distribution, mais forte dépendance à la période d’observation.

questions.q: A fund returned 11% with a volatility of 15%. The risk-free rate is 2%. What is its Sharpe ratio?
An investor allocates a small part of a well-diversified portfolio to a hedge fund. Which ratio is most appropriate to evaluate that fund’s contribution?
questions.explain: Dans un portefeuille bien diversifié, seul le risque **systématique** compte : le **Treynor** (ou l’alpha de Jensen) est adapté. Le Sharpe convient quand le portefeuille représente toute la richesse.

questions.q: A portfolio returned 9% with a beta of 0.8. The market returned 10% and the risk-free rate is 2%. What is Jensen’s alpha?
A manager returned 8.5% versus 7% for her benchmark, with a tracking error of 3%. What is the information ratio?
Why might the Sharpe ratio of a strategy that systematically sells out-of-the-money options be misleading?
options: Low measured volatility hides rare but large losses (negative skew)
Its returns are always positively skewed
The strategy has no exposure to volatility
The Sharpe ratio penalizes upside volatility too little
questions.explain: Vendre des options procure des gains réguliers et une faible volatilité mesurée… jusqu’au krach. Le Sharpe ignore l’**asymétrie négative** et les queues épaisses : il est surestimé.

questions.q: The Sortino ratio is preferable to the Sharpe ratio when:
options: Returns are asymmetric and the investor is concerned mainly with downside risk
The portfolio is a small part of a diversified portfolio
Comparing a manager to a benchmark
questions.explain: Le **Sortino** ne pénalise que la volatilité sous la cible : utile pour des rendements asymétriques et des investisseurs sensibles aux pertes.

questions.q: An analyst concludes that a manager generates alpha when, in fact, the manager has no skill. This is a:
questions.explain: Rejeter à tort l’hypothèse nulle (« pas d’alpha ») = **erreur de type I** (faux positif).

questions.q: A regression estimates a monthly alpha of 0.40% with a standard error of 0.25%. At the 5% significance level (critical value 1.96), the analyst should:
options: Fail to reject the null hypothesis that alpha is zero
Reject the null hypothesis that alpha is zero
questions.explain: $t = 0{,}40/0{,}25 = 1{,}6 < 1{,}96$ : on **ne rejette pas** $H_0$. L’alpha n’est pas statistiquement significatif.

questions.q: A quant tests 500 trading rules on the same 10-year data set and reports the best one, which has a t-statistic of 3.1. The main concern is:
options: Low statistical power from too many observations
Look-ahead bias in the risk-free rate
questions.explain: En testant 500 règles, certaines paraîtront significatives **par hasard** : c’est le surapprentissage / data mining. Il faut un test hors échantillon ou des seuils plus exigeants.

questions.q: A long-only small-cap value fund shows a large, significant alpha in a single-factor CAPM regression, but no alpha in a regression including size and value factors. The CAPM alpha most likely reflects:
questions.explain: L’alpha CAPM provenait de facteurs **omis** (taille, value). Une fois ces bêtas pris en compte, il disparaît : c’était un faux alpha.

questions.q: A high R² in a regression of a fund’s returns on market factors indicates that:
options: Most of the fund’s return variation is explained by the factors
The fund has a large alpha
The fund is uncorrelated with the factors
questions.explain: Le **R²** mesure la part de la variance expliquée par les facteurs. Un R² élevé signifie un fonds proche de ses bêtas (peu de risque spécifique).

questions.q: A fund has an up-market beta of 0.3 and a down-market beta of 0.9. A single linear beta estimated over all periods will most likely:
questions.explain: Bêta **asymétrique** : la moyenne (≈ 0,6) sous-estime l’exposition en marché baissier (0,9). Les modèles linéaires captent mal les profils optionnels.

questions.q: A high-water mark provision ensures that:
options: Incentive fees are paid only on gains above the previous peak NAV
Investors can redeem at the highest NAV
The manager earns a fee on every positive month
questions.explain: Avec un **high-water mark**, le gérant doit d’abord récupérer les pertes passées avant de toucher une commission de performance.

questions.q: With a 20% incentive fee and an 8% hurdle, a fund earns 12%. Ignoring management fees, the incentive fee equals 2.4% under a soft hurdle (with full catch-up) and, under a hard hurdle, equals:
questions.explain: **Hard hurdle** : 20 % × (12 % − 8 %) = 0,8 %. **Soft hurdle** : une fois le seuil dépassé, 20 % × 12 % = 2,4 %.

questions.q: Viewing the incentive fee as a call option held by the manager, what effect does an increase in fund volatility have?
options: It increases the value of the manager’s incentive fee option
It decreases the value of the option
It converts the option into a put
questions.explain: Comme toute option, la commission de performance **vaut plus** si la volatilité augmente : incitation potentielle à prendre plus de risques.

questions.q: A hedge fund is 30% below its high-water mark. Which behavior is the incentive structure most likely to encourage?
options: Increasing risk or closing the fund and launching a new one
Reducing leverage to protect the remaining NAV
questions.explain: L’option est très **hors de la monnaie** : le gérant peut être tenté d’augmenter le risque, ou de fermer le fonds pour repartir sans high-water mark.

questions.q: A fund lost 20% last year. With a high-water mark, what return must it earn this year (gross) before it can charge an incentive fee?
questions.explain: $0{,}8 \times (1+R) = 1 \Rightarrow R = 25\%$.

questions.q: In a private equity fund, a clawback provision requires that:
options: The GP returns carried interest received in excess of its entitlement over the fund’s life
LPs return distributions if the fund needs more capital
The GP pays a penalty for late capital calls
Management fees are refunded if the fund loses money
questions.explain: Le **clawback** oblige le GP à restituer le carry trop perçu (par exemple après des pertes sur des investissements tardifs).

questions.q: A hedge fund limits total redemptions in any quarter to 10% of fund assets. This provision is called a:
questions.explain: La **gate** plafonne les rachats par période. Le lockup interdit les rachats pendant une période initiale ; le side pocket isole des actifs illiquides.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a side pocket?
options: To isolate illiquid or hard-to-value assets so that redeeming and new investors are treated fairly
To pay incentive fees in advance
questions.explain: Le **side pocket** sépare les actifs illiquides : les investisseurs sortants ne sont pas payés à une valeur incertaine, et les nouveaux n’achètent pas ces actifs à un prix arbitraire.

questions.q: In a limited partnership, the limited partners:
options: Provide capital and have liability limited to their investment
questions.explain: Les **LP** apportent le capital avec une responsabilité limitée. Le **GP** gère, a une responsabilité illimitée et perçoit le carry.

questions.q: A portfolio holds 90% in assets with 10% volatility and 10% in bitcoin with 60% volatility. The correlation is 0.2. Portfolio volatility is closest to:
questions.explain: $\sigma^2 = 0{,}9^2 \times 0{,}10^2 + 0{,}1^2 \times 0{,}60^2 + 2 \times 0{,}9 \times 0{,}1 \times 0{,}2 \times 0{,}10 \times 0{,}60 = 0{,}0081 + 0{,}0036 + 0{,}00216 = 0{,}01386$, donc $\sigma = \sqrt{0{,}01386} \approx 11{,}8\%$. Une petite poche très volatile mais peu corrélée n’augmente que modérément le risque total.
